is swung in an arc so its face strikes squarely
can leave a round dent in a surface when it misses
makes a loud bang with every blow it lands

has a handle of hickory, fibreglass or solid metal

has a flat blade set at a right angle to its handle

is pulled back toward the user in short scraping strokes

clause: loosens soil between rows of vegetables in a garden

is kept in a garden shed alongside spades and forks
has its blade edge sharpened with a flat file
can open a shallow trench for planting seeds

breaks up hard crusted earth after heavy rain
has a thin metal blade with one sharpened edge
slices bread, meat and vegetables on a cutting board
is set on the dinner table beside the plate
comes in folding versions that fit in a pocket
R2_comment: Folding versions that fit in a pocket strongly identify a pocketknife.

clause: needs regular sharpening on a whetstone or grinder
is washed by hand rather than in a dishwasher to stay sharp
drafter_note: "is washed by hand rather than in a dishwasher to stay sharp": standard advice for good kitchen knives; many households put everyday knives in the dishwasher
R2_comment: Hand washing is care advice for good kitchen knives, not a general practice or requirement for all knives.

clause: has a finely serrated edge on some of its types
has a pointed tip for piercing and making small cuts
R2_comment: Pointed piercing tips depend on type; ordinary table and butter knives can be rounded.

clause: is carried by hunters and campers on a belt
has a handle fixed to its blade with rivets on many types
spreads jam or margarine onto toast at breakfast
is drawn away from the body when cutting to avoid injury
has an absorbent head on the end of a long handle

is wrung out to get rid of dirty water
is swept across hard floors in wide side-to-side strokes
is used by school janitors to clean corridors and restrooms
leaves floors wet enough to need a warning sign nearby
has a detachable head that can go in a washing machine
R2_comment: A detachable machine-washable head is model-dependent; sponge and other heads may not be washable this way.

clause: is used by sailors to wash down a ship's deck
can have a flat head covered in microfibre cloth
is stored upright in a utility closet to dry

is used to repair torn clothing at home

is made of thin polished metal a few centimetres long
is used in crafts such as quilting and beading

has a long handle about as tall as an adult

is sold with wide or narrow heads for different jobs
has a row of sharp teeth along a thin metal blade

R2_comment: A hand-saw description; common powered or rotary saws do not cut by a back-and-forth arm stroke.

clause: leaves a small pile of fine dust on the floor
is often hung on a pegboard in a woodworking shop

has a closed handle at one end of a long tapering blade
can cut through metal pipe as well as timber
is sharpened with a small file rather than a flat stone

clause: cuts on the pull stroke in some designs and the push in others
R2_comment: Pull-cut versus push-cut designs are a characteristic saw identification cue.

clause: has two blades joined by a pivot near the middle
has two handles that one hand squeezes and opens
cuts cleanly through thin sheets with each closing stroke
is found in school pencil cases for craft lessons
is kept at a barber's station along with combs and clippers

clause: is kept out of reach of small children because of its points
is made in special versions for left-handed people
is used in kitchens to cut herbs and open packaging
is used to cut cloth, twine and gift wrapping
R2_comment: Cutting cloth, twine and wrapping together strongly identifies scissors.

clause: is found in first aid kits, desk drawers and sewing baskets
R2_comment: The combined first-aid, desk and sewing-basket contexts strongly identify scissors.

clause: makes a crisp metallic sound each time it closes
R2_comment: A crisp metallic sound is not guaranteed each time scissors close; many close quietly.

clause: loses its edge quickly if used to cut wire
has a spiral thread wound around a pointed shaft
has a flat or rounded head at one end of its shaft

R2_comment: Ordinary right-hand thread convention; exceptional left-hand threads do not defeat this generic description.

can be set below the surface and hidden with filler

clause: is often sold by gauge and length in boxes of a hundred
drafter_note: "is often sold by gauge and length in boxes of a hundred": gauge sizing is the imperial wood-screw convention; metric screws are sold by diameter
R2_comment: 'Often' accommodates imperial gauge sizing without excluding metric sizes.

clause: becomes hard to remove once its head is damaged
fastens hinges and handles to doors and cabinets
is tiny in eyeglass frames and wristwatches
R2_comment: The tiny fasteners in eyeglass frames and wristwatches strongly point to screws.

clause: has a broad curved blade on the end of a long handle
is pushed into the ground with a foot on its blade
moves loose piles of gravel, sand or mulch
has a D-shaped grip at the top of its handle on some models
clears snow from driveways and paths in winter

tosses dirt to one side in a lifting swing
often has a pointed blade for breaking into hard ground
scoops ash out of a fireplace or stove
is used alongside a wheelbarrow to move earth
has a flat or dished blade for scraping and scooping
is soft and porous and soaks up water when dipped
is squeezed in the hand to wring out dirty water
has a rougher side for scrubbing stuck-on grime
R2_comment: A separate rough scrubbing side depends on the cleaning-sponge type; many are uniformly soft.

clause: sits in a small holder beside the kitchen sink
wipes crumbs and spills off countertops and tables
is made from synthetic foam or processed plant fibre
R2_comment: Synthetic foam and plant fibre cover common manufactured types, but natural sea sponges are also used for cleaning.

clause: can breed bacteria when it stays damp for days
is cut into rectangular blocks that fit in a hand
R2_comment: Fits the ordinary manufactured kitchen sponge as a generic description.

clause: is used with soapy water to wash a car body
stiffens when dry and softens again once wet
drafter_note: "stiffens when dry and softens again once wet": true of cellulose sponges; polyurethane foam sponges stay fairly soft when dry
R2_comment: Dry stiffening is characteristic of cellulose sponges, not all foam types.

clause: is thrown away and replaced every few weeks for hygiene
drafter_note: "is thrown away and replaced every few weeks for hygiene": common hygiene advice (weekly to monthly), not what every household does
R2_comment: A replacement recommendation rather than a general fact about household practice; reusable types also vary.

clause: is rubbed on dishes with washing-up liquid to scrub them
is mounted on a workbench in many home garages
has two heavy parallel jaws that grip a workpiece
is tightened by turning a handle on a threaded shaft
is used to bend flat bar by gripping one end
often has a swivel base so it can be turned to any angle
can weigh over twenty kilograms on large models
drafter_note: "can weigh over twenty kilograms on large models": large engineer's bench vises (150 mm jaws and up) are in this range; small hobby vises weigh a few kilograms
R2_comment: 'Can' and 'large models' properly qualify the weight.

clause: is made of heavy cast iron or forged metal
has ridged gripping faces that can mark soft work
R2_comment: Serrated jaws fit many metalworking vises; woodworking and soft-jaw versions can have smooth gripping faces.

clause: holds a part steady so both hands are free to work on it
can grip round pipe as well as flat stock
is found in metalworking and woodworking shops alike
comes in small precision versions for jewellers and model makers
has loops of thin wire gathered into a handle
adds air to a mixture to make it light and fluffy
is moved quickly in circles with a flick of the wrist
makes a rapid clattering sound against the side of a bowl
is used to stir sauces and gravy on the stove
is wider at its working end than at its handle
hangs from a hook in the kitchen with other utensils
R2_comment: 'Utensils' names the tools family by a kitchen-context synonym.

clause: is used by bakers to mix cake and pancake batters
is often swapped for an electric mixer on big batches
comes in a flat version suited to shallow pans
is made of metal or heat-resistant silicone
needs careful rinsing because thick mixture clings to it
grows on trees in orchards and is picked in autumn
has crisp white flesh under a thin red, green or yellow skin
has a few small seeds that are usually discarded before cooking
has a short stem sitting in a small dip at the top
turns brown quickly once its cut flesh meets the air
is often pressed into a sweet juice sold in cartons
is baked into sweet pies, tarts and crumbles
keeps for months in cool, controlled storage after harvest
comes in many varieties ranging from sweet to sharp
is eaten raw as a crunchy snack, often skin and all
is stewed with sugar until soft and served warm
is packed in lunchboxes as an easy whole piece of fruit
grows in large hanging bunches on tall tropical plants
has a mild, sweet, slightly starchy taste
gets brown speckles on its skin as it becomes very ripe
has soft, pale, creamy flesh that is easy to mash

is picked while still green and shipped to ripen later
is blended into smoothies to make them thick and sweet
is sliced over breakfast cereal or porridge
has tiny dark specks of seed running through its centre
drafter_note: "has tiny dark specks of seed running through its centre" - in seedless dessert bananas the specks are undeveloped vestigial seeds; a reader may not think of them as seeds
R2_comment: The tiny dark specks can reasonably be called vestigial/undeveloped seeds in ordinary language.

clause: is served with ice cream or custard as a simple dessert
is best kept at room temperature rather than in the fridge
R2_comment: Room temperature is appropriate for ripening; refrigeration can extend storage once ripe. 'Best' depends on ripeness and purpose.

clause: is made from cream and sold in the chilled aisle
R2_comment: Made from cream and sold chilled strongly identifies butter.

clause: is pale yellow and firm when it comes out of the fridge
softens at room temperature and melts quickly in a warm pan
is spread thinly on warm toast or fresh bread
comes salted or unsalted in wrapped rectangular blocks
is weighed out for cakes and biscuits in most home baking
R2_comment: Use in 'most home baking' depends on recipe and culture; oil and other fats are also common.

clause: is melted and brushed over dough before baking
is about four-fifths milk fat by weight
drafter_note: "is about four-fifths milk fat by weight" - 80% is the legal minimum in the US and EU; European-style butters run to about 82-86%
R2_comment: 'About four-fifths' allows the usual modest variation in milk-fat content.

clause: can scorch and turn bitter if heated too long
is rubbed into flour to make pastry and crumble toppings
is stirred into hot mashed potatoes to make them rich
is mixed with garlic and herbs as a topping for grilled meat

clause: is often aged for weeks, months or years in cool cellars
has a firm outer rind that is often cut away
R2_comment: Many ordinary fresh or processed cheeses have no firm outer rind.

clause: softens and turns gooey when heated in the oven
R2_comment: Melting to a gooey texture depends on type; paneer and halloumi are ordinary counterexamples.

clause: is grated over hot dishes or sliced thinly for sandwiches
can be made from the milk of goats or water buffalo as well
comes in many regional styles with protected local names
can have a strong smell that some people find off-putting
is eaten with crackers, bread or slices of fruit
is wrapped tightly and kept in the fridge after opening
is made with the help of friendly bacteria
R2_comment: Some fresh cheeses are directly acid-set; bacterial cultures are not required for every cheese type.

clause: is salted in brine or rubbed with salt to preserve it
R2_comment: Salting varies: salt may be mixed into curds, and some fresh cheeses are unsalted, rather than brined or surface-rubbed.

clause: is sold in free-range and organic versions at higher prices
is a cheap and versatile source of protein

is boiled for a few minutes to be eaten soft or hard

is poached in a pan of gently simmering water

changes from runny to firm as it cooks
sinks in a glass of water when fresh and floats when stale
drafter_note: "sinks in a glass of water when fresh and floats when stale" - the standard kitchen test; ageing eggs usually tilt or stand on end before they actually float
R2_comment: Read 'stale' as aged, not a reliable diagnosis of spoilage; the familiar test reflects growth of the air cell.

clause: is smooth and roughly oval, fitting easily in the palm
R2_comment: A smooth palm-sized oval supplies a strong ordinary egg identification cue.

clause: grows on climbing vines trained along wires in long rows
R2_comment: Climbing vines trained in long wired rows strongly identify vineyard grapes.

clause: is small, round and juicy with a smooth thin skin
comes in green, red and dark purple varieties

is toxic to dogs even in small amounts
drafter_note: "is toxic to dogs even in small amounts" - toxicity is well established but idiosyncratic; some dogs eat a few without harm
R2_comment: Toxicity to dogs at small amounts is a recognizable grape cue. Variable susceptibility does not negate the hazard.

clause: is pressed into a juice or cooked into a sweet jelly
is used as a natural sweetener in place of sugar
is thick, sticky and amber in colour
keeps almost indefinitely in a sealed jar without spoiling
drafter_note: "keeps almost indefinitely in a sealed jar without spoiling" - true of properly ripened low-moisture honey; high-moisture honey can ferment
R2_comment: Read as ordinary properly ripened, low-moisture honey; 'almost' appropriately qualifies storage life.

clause: can turn grainy if stored too long or too cold
is stirred into hot tea to sweeten it
is spread on toast, crumpets or warm scones
comes in dark, strong kinds and pale, mild kinds
is sold in glass jars and squeezable bottles

is added to marinades and glazes for roast meat

is added to hot water or tea for a sharp flavour
grows on small, thorny evergreen trees in warm climates
drafter_note: "grows on small, thorny evergreen trees in warm climates" - most lemon cultivars bear thorns, but some are nearly thornless
R2_comment: A normal generic citrus-tree description; it need not exclude the nearly thornless cultivars.

clause: is high in vitamin C but low in natural sugar

is mixed with oil to dress salads in place of vinegar
is oval with a small pointed tip at one or both ends

has sap near the stem that can irritate the skin
drafter_note: "has sap near the stem that can irritate the skin" - the sap contains urushiol-related compounds; it affects sensitive people, not everyone
R2_comment: 'Can irritate' correctly allows individual sensitivity rather than asserting everyone reacts.

clause: is a round citrus fruit with a thick, dimpled peel

drafter_note: "has a peel that can stay green on the tree in the tropics" - true (colour change needs cool nights), but may not be common knowledge to a reader
R2_comment: Ripe oranges can remain green under tropical growing conditions.

R2_comment: Orange blossom is used in perfume; the claim does not require every cultivar to supply the trade.

clause: is roughly the size of a tennis ball or a little bigger

is baked in minutes in a blazing hot stone oven

R2_comment: Wedge slicing together with hand eating strongly identifies pizza.

clause: is a popular takeaway ordered by phone or app
is often bought by the slice and eaten on the go
R2_comment: Buying a slice to eat on the go is a characteristic pizza cue.

clause: has a crust that may be thin and crisp or thick and chewy

clause: can be blended smooth or left chunky with pieces
R2_comment: The familiar smooth-blended versus chunky distinction strongly identifies soup.

clause: is served with crusty bread for dipping

is cooked slowly in a large pot on the stove

R2_comment: 'Seeds' is normal everyday terminology for the external achenes.

clause: turns bright red all over when fully ripe

R2_comment: The small removable green-leaf tuft is a recognizable strawberry cue.

clause: grows on low, leafy plants close to the ground

clause: is a popular flavour for milkshakes, yoghurt and ice cream
is soft and juicy with a sweet, slightly tart taste
is built around small portions of cooked, seasoned rice
is topped or rolled with raw fish such as salmon or tuna

clause: is often wrapped in thin sheets of dried seaweed

is eaten with chopsticks or simply by hand
comes with a sharp, hot condiment on the side
is cut into bite-sized rounds from a long roll

clause: is prepared by chefs who spend years learning the craft
is sold in ready-made packs at supermarket chilled counters
was first developed as a way to preserve fish
drafter_note: "was first developed as a way to preserve fish" - refers to narezushi, fish packed in fermenting rice; accurate but not everyday knowledge
R2_comment: The preservation origin refers to fermented-fish-and-rice predecessors.

clause: can be filled with avocado and cucumber instead of meat

is often run by a public transport authority
drafter_note: "is often run by a public transport authority" - many ferries are public, but many are privately operated; 'often' carries the claim
R2_comment: 'Often' permits the common privately operated ferries.

clause: sounds a deep horn before it pulls away from the dock
is usually driven by propellers turned by diesel engines
carries commuters to islands that have no bridge to the mainland

R2_comment: A bridge high above passenger decks describes larger ferries, not many small passenger or river ferries.

clause: can be big enough to carry hundreds of passengers at once
